pr_title: systemd-sysext: Implement optional mutability for extensions
pr_body:
The PR implements some parts of the proposed update to the Extension Images specifications - https://github.com/uapi-group/specifications/pull/78 - implemented are minimal requirements for enabling mutability and the `--mutable` command line flag. There is no configurability through config files. There is no ephemeral mode.

Fixes: #31392

```
fedora kernel: overlayfs: ...falling back to uuid=null.
fedora kernel: overlayfs: try mounting with 'userxattr' option
```

Edit: Here the docs: `User xattr: The "-o userxattr" mount option forces overlayfs to use the "user.overlay." xattr namespace instead of "trusted.overlay.". This is useful for unprivileged mounting of overlayfs.`

How would the ephemeral option work? The workdir needs to be in the same mount point, so it won't work to directly have the `etc.local` (or how it's named) subdirectly as tmpfs, but with the current logic that looks for the parent dir to create the workdir it would need to be the whole parent dir that's a tmpfs¹ - not so good if we want to manage etc and usr differently. I think it could work by having the `etc.local` entry point to a specific symlink (`/dev/null`?) and handling this special case by setting up a tmpfs elsewhere that contains the ephemeral etc.local and the workdir used for the overlay. Doing it this way would also allow to overwrite behavior in the command line flag: The original `etc.local` entry stays as is and we set up a tmpfs mount containing the ephemeral upperdir and workdir for the overlay.

¹ I tried `/var/lib/extension-data` as tmpfs and got `Assertion 'prefix' failed at src/basic/path-util.c:408, function path_startswith_full(). Aborting.` - not sure if we would support that, I think it's better to create the mounts explicitly in the code.

issue_context.title: mutable /etc/ leayers in confext
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

254.9-1.fc39

### Used distribution

uBlue/Bazzite

### Linux kernel version used

6.7.4-204.fsync.fc39.x86_64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd-confext

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

Keeping the `/etc` tree R/W for the admin, minus the actual files inside the `confext` which would be R/O as expected.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

A single `confext` merged into the system will render the whole `/etc` OS-tree __Read-Only__.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Create a simple `confext` with one service file/conf inside it, in proper tree-struture, along with a `extension-release` file.
_(For ease i used a directory instead of a raw image)_
1. `sudo systemd-confext merge`
1. `sudo touch /etc/test123` <-- will give an error.
1. `sudo systemd-confext unmerge` to revert.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

_No response_
comments:
As an end-user, one expects that only the parts inside the `confext` that get "merged" into the system will be R/O, while the rest of `/etc` remains R/W for the admin to alter as wanted as usual.
But as-is this functionality locks the whole `/etc` OS-tree which is NOT what any end-user of this functionality expects. (despite it being mentioned in the docs briefly somewhere)
@TriMoon You might be interested in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/31000 :wink:

@t-lo Yea i noticed that and commented in https://github.com/uapi-group/specifications/pull/78#issuecomment-1952611735 already as you saw :+1: 
although the optional R/W in that topic might be something that could be wanted, in this topic `/etc` should stay R/W by default don't you agree? :wink:

> As an end-user, one expects that only the parts inside the `confext` that get "merged" into the system will be R/O, while the rest of `/etc` remains R/W for the admin to alter as wanted as usual.
> But as-is this functionality locks the whole `/etc` OS-tree which is NOT what any end-user of this functionality expects. (despite it being mentioned in the docs briefly somewhere)

sysext/confext are not really "end-user" facing. They are tools for OS builders really. Yeah, traditional desktop systems and the tools for that expect to be able to write to arbitrary files in /etc/, but confext is not really designed with that usecase in mind. With #31000 things will be opened up a bit, for specific usecases, but that's still not primarily focussed on a desktop usecase.

I mean, what are you using confext for, if I may ask? What's your specific usecase?

The concept was implemented with immutable OS in mind, which want to extend the immutability to /etc/ and ensure it's always a combination of various immutable images. With #31000 this is opened up a bit, so that on top of all that you can also have a mutable layer, but at it's core it's focussed on OSes which care about immutability (cryptographic even, dm-verity and stuff), hence I am curious what you intend to use it for?

@poettering 
> sysext/confext are not really "end-user" facing.

By end-user in that sentence's context i actually meant the local admin being the end-user of this functionality...

> The concept was implemented with immutable OS in mind, which want to extend the immutability to /etc/ and ensure it's always a combination of various immutable images.

That could be done in the `initrd` phase to mount `/etc` R/O if so desired, which i would not agree with either... :woman_shrugging: 

I don't quite understand why using a feature, that can overlay stuff inside a neatly distributed raw image, would render the `/etc` tree R/O which is in principle designed to give the local admin freedom to make changes in.
It's like turning `/tmp` R/O, which goes against it's usage-purpose...


> I mean, what are you using confext for, if I may ask? What's your specific usecase?

My goal was to be able to "package" certain configurations under `/etc` in a locked-down form, but keep the spirit of the `/etc` tree R/W.
Thus only the parts of the applied `confext` would be "locked-down".
The current state as-is, is just all R/O or not :disappointed:

By the way i just noticed you changed the title, but...

This topic is about leaving the whole `/etc` OS-tree R/W, while you guys in that other topic try to keep the applied parts from a `sysext` R/W.
These are two independent different usages...

> This topic is about leaving the whole /etc OS-tree R/W, while you guys in that other topic try to keep the applied parts inside a sysext R/W.

The PR referenced above introduces "write routing" via directories (or symlinks) in `/var/lib/extensions.mutable/[etc|usr|opt]` so the base OS remains mutable even when extensions are merged. The sysexts itself are not changed (and in many cases can't, e.g. when they are shipped in a squashfs). For your use case (`/etc` mutable) one would create a symlink `/var/lib/extensions.mutable/etc → /etc`.

(BTW. we have the exact same `/etc` use case in Flatcar, which is one of the main motivators for this work. We currently use a custom overlay mount which we'd like to move away from).

I don't think the solution to a problem is to create bypasses for a flaw in the original implementation...
IMHO, it's better to fix/change the original to not have this flaw in the first place, in my point of view...

---
To use that "write routing" functionality, one would be forced to always use `sysext` in combination with `confext`, which in practice would mean not using any of them but instead use portable-services...

It's not a bypass - this is how overlayfs works: it uses an optional "upper" layer in the FS stack that takes writes. Overlayfs results in a read-only mount if no upperdir is specified. sysexts did not make use of upperdirs until now; the PR changes that.

The write routing directories are merely a means of configuring the "upperdir". The spec [defines 3 different ways](https://github.com/uapi-group/specifications/pull/78/files#diff-5206e28079f81595cf12ac61766e5e1065568eee7acc5cab7b5757a3048a906dR95-R108) of configuring the upperdir; the PR implements the (mandatory) 1st option.

> To use that "write routing" functionality, one would be forced to always use sysext in combination with confext, which in practice would mean not using any of them but instead use portable-services...

Write routing does not distinguish between sysexts and confexts. You can happily run it in `confext merge --mutable=auto` mode and only create a symlink for `/etc`, and there won't be any impact for / need to use sysexts.

> It's not a bypass - this is how overlayfs works: it uses an optional "upper" layer in the FS stack that takes writes. Overlayfs results in a read-only mount if no upperdir is specified. sysexts did not make use of upperdirs until now; the PR changes that.

Maybe that is the flaw here...
Instead of overlayfs for the whole tree, they maybe need to use internal bind-mount's (or similar) that only "overlay" the specific files from the respective `confext`

> Instead of overlayfs for the whole tree, they maybe need to use internal bind-mount's (or similar) that only "overlay" the specific files from the respective `confext`

Sysexts / confexts were conceived with immutable Linux distributions in mind, and our mutability feature only covers some edge cases where all-out immutability is not (yet) desirable. One of the cornerstones of extensions is their simplicity - a single overlayfs mount - which makes the feature very robust and secure.
For shipping sub-trees / individual files there are better options available than overlayfs mounts; the management overhead of handling arbitrary sub-trees would be hard to justify against these.

> I don't quite understand why using a feature, that can overlay stuff inside a neatly distributed raw image, would render the `/etc` tree R/O which is in principle designed to give the local admin freedom to make changes in.

On desktop systems a writable /etc/ is expected, but on appliances, servers not necessarily. Many consider it a problem even, and prefer that /etc/ exclusively consists of properly authenticated confexts, with no chance of local modifications, so that an attacker simply cannot modify anything to gain persistency.

> It's like turning `/tmp` R/O, which goes against it's usage-purpose...

Nope. /tmp/ must be writable to be useful, but /etc/ not so much. Depending on the usecase not allowing mutability of /etc/ might generally be preferable, and most userspace doesn#t need it anyway, as they are consumer of /etc/, not manager of it.

> This topic is about leaving the whole `/etc` OS-tree R/W, while you guys in that other topic try to keep the applied parts from a `sysext` R/W.
> These are two independent different usages...

sysext/confext are implemented via overlayfs, and overlayfs currently has not mechanism for allowing inodes from certain layers to remain immutable while prohibiting this for inodes from other layers.

I have proposed this personally to some kernel fs people already, but don#t hold your breath.

@poettering 
> Many consider it a problem even, and prefer that /etc/ exclusively consists of properly authenticated confexts, with no chance of local modifications, so that an attacker simply cannot modify anything to gain persistency.

That's exactly where `confext` can "lockdown" specific stuff in `/etc` that are expected to stay in an authenticated state and immutable...

I think i don't have to point out that there are other places that provide persistency... _(fe. `/var/`)_
Unless they want that tree to be R/O also, in which case they might as-well throw away the whole R/W functionality of the OS for the normal filesystems...


> Nope. /tmp/ must be writable to be useful, but /etc/ not so much.

From a vendor's point of view maybe, but not from a local admin's point of view. (The machine owner and operator)
Like i already pointed out, in those scenarios where it would be desirable to have a R/O `/etc` they can create an `initrd` that mounts the `/etc` OS-tree in such a R/O way by explicit choice.

> sysext/confext are implemented via overlayfs, and overlayfs currently has not mechanism for allowing inodes from certain layers to remain immutable while prohibiting this for inodes from other layers.

I have understand that by now, that's why i suggested you to use `bind-mount's` for the `confext` functionality.

Well ofcourse i don't know how much an impact it would have with respect to the overhead of `bind-mount`ing single files individually.

_(By "the rest" i mean anything that was not part of the final result of the respective `confext` image or dir)_

And, IMHO, that overhead would mostly only occur when accessing the respective files that need extra handling right?

PS: @poettering i would appriciate if you would rename the title back, because this issue is NOT about having mutable layers inside a `confext`...

i don't understand what bind mounts have to do with overlay mounts? binds mounts just make some inode appear at multiple places along with any children in case the inode is a dir. overlay mounts however merger trees, and can thus augment new inodes at arbitrary places.

Also overlayfs as this nice atomic behaviour, either it's there in full, or not at all. there's never a half setup. Which is ideal

@poettering , first off excuses for leaving this discussion mid-way, but i had to sleep :smiley_cat: 

> i don't understand what you are looking for then?
> i don't understand what bind mounts have to do with overlay mounts?

Let me explain in a more verbose way then if i can:

Currently:
- You combine the `/etc` tree of the destination `OS-tree` with the `/etc` tree of the `confext` using `overlayfs`.
- This causes the `/etc` tree on the host to become R/O.

What i mean/ask to happen is:

@TriMoon  What you're asking for is precisely what's implemented by #31000 .

> current overlayfs way:
> `Image_A` is the base OS-tree. (the lower image layer?)

Plain old `/etc` on the root fs basically. Lowerdir in overlayfs lingo.

> This image is mutable (R/W) per definition because it is on the drive of the end-user (or in RAM using tempfs).

 Not _by definition_ (both Lennart and Luca gave examples where this is not the case) but let's assume for our case at hand it is.

> `Image_B` is the contents of the sysext/confext. (the upper image layer?)
> This image is immutable (R/O) by definition of the functionality of sysext/confext.

The middle layer(s). _Also_ called lowerdir in overlayfs lingo (there can be many lowerdirs).

> The viewer is looking at the combination of the two from the top towards the bottom: Viewer ⇒ `Image_B` ⇒ `Image_A`
> The viewer can see pixels (files) from `Image_A` if they are in spots that are not occupied in `Image_B`.
> `Image_B` acts like hard-glass where the viewer can see through but not change anything on, which also makes `Image_A` unchangeable / immutable / (R/O) from this angle of view, because you access the result from top-to-bottom 
(through the hard-glass).
> That is why there is a need to create a mutable `Image_C` that needs to be placed on top of Image_B to make the total result mutable again, which is called the workdir.
> (Current sysext/confext does not use a workdir)
>Correct so far?

No. First of all, in sysexts as currently implemented, both `Image_A` and `Image_B` are lowerdirs. Additionally, `Image_A` is the _mount point_. Mounts are opaque, but since `Image_A` is part of the stack, it will _look like_ you can see thorugh.

One can _optionally_ specify an upperdir to overlayfs.  _If specified_, that's where the writes go. But it is optional. So if you don't specify an upper layer at all (like sysext implementation currently), your resulting merged overlayfs mount will be immutable.

So you stack the _lowerdirs_, and then mount them where `Image_A` happens to reside in the file system. The mount point is opaque - if you mount anything over a directory with contents, then the contents will disappear, hidden by whatever is mounted. However, since `Image_A` is _also_ part of the overlayfs stack, it will "look like" you can see through `Image_B`. 

Because there is no upperdir specified, the mount will result in a read-only filesystem:
* `<mount point which happens to be the position of Image_A in the file system>`
* `Image_B` (lowerdir)
* `Image_A` (lowerdir)

If you run `mount` on a system with sysexts merged you'll see
```
...
sysext on /usr type overlay (ro,relatime,seclabel,lowerdir=/run/systemd/sysext/meta/usr:/run/systemd/sysext/extensions/oem-qemu/usr:/run/systemd/sysext/extensions/docker-flatcar/usr:/run/systemd/sysext/extensions/containerd-flatcar/usr:/usr)
...
```
This is on the latest Flatcar alpha which ships containerd and docker as sysexts. As you see there is _only_ `lowerdir=`, no `upperdir=` or `workdir=`.

#31000 extends this.

If you specify the `--mutable` option, the overlayfs mount will now use an upperdir. Upperdirs take writes, and the overlayfs mount thus will be writable. The directories in `/var/extensions.mutable/...` are used to set up the upperdir.

To get back to your image example:
* If  `/var/extensions.mutable/etc` is a directory, it will be the upperdir. The stack is then
   * `Image_C`  (upperdir, `/var/extensions.mutable/etc`)
   * `Image_B` (lowerdir)
   * `Image_A` (lowerdir)
* If  `/var/extensions.mutable/etc` is a _symlink_ to `/etc`; then `/etc` (aka `Image_A`) will be the upperdir. The stack is then
   * `Image_A`  (upperdir, `/etc`)
   * `Image_B` (lowerdir)

Just FYI, the overlayfs feature idea is tracked in the https://uapi-group.org/kernel-features/ list:
> `overlayfs` should permit *immutable* layers, i.e. layers whose non-directory inodes may not be overriden in an upper writable layer.

Edit: To be clear, for root it will of course still be possible to circumvent this through a bunch of ways - one can create a file explicitly in original filesystem of the upperdir, or one could bind mount things on top to overwrite, one can remount without this feature etc - The main idea is to prevent accidental upcopies when tools are not aware of the wanted immutability and with this feature we could let the modifying syscalls fail.
